summary:
In less than four months, from June 24 to October 10, 2026, the NISAR radar of NASA and ISRO saw 938 hectares of the Andes in Ayacucho lose their vegetation. In Huanta, Huamanga and La Mar, farming families lose soil and crops to erosion, wildfires, droughts and earthquakes, on hillsides with almost no internet access.

GAIA RIKCHAY is a system that turns real NISAR data into decisions. It compares the radar signal before and after, maps 498 damaged zones and cross-checks each one with soil moisture, heat hotspots, earthquakes, slope and soil type. It then explains what is happening in each zone, always with its source and date, and asks for field verification when the evidence is not enough.

GAIA RIKCHAY doesn’t just alert, it acts. For each zone, it proposes a path to heal the land with native plants such as queñua, aliso (Andean alder), cabuya and ichu grass. It says which technique to use, when to plant and who does the work, through the minka, a traditional Andean form of community work. It also creates bulletins for community radio in Spanish, with a Quechua version under review, to reach families without internet.

We turn complex data into practical decisions for farmers and authorities, to protect harvests and build a resilient future.
details:
PROJECT GAIA

uses NASA’s NISAR radar to see where the land in the Andes is losing life, and tells each community what to do to heal it. In Ayacucho, it detected 938 hectares of vegetation lost in just four months, spread across 498 zones.

How does it work?

See: it compares radar images from two dates and marks the damaged zones.

Explain: it cross-checks each zone with moisture, wildfire, earthquake and soil data to show what happened.

Act: it recommends which native plants to grow, when to plant and who does the work through the minka, and prepares an alert for community radio.

Benefits

  • Clear information for farming families and local authorities.
  • It reaches places without internet, through radio and the minka.
  • Every piece of data shows its source and date.

Expected impact
Protecting soil and harvests from wildfires, droughts, mudslides and landslides with low-cost, nature-based solutions carried out by the community itself. It works in any area of the Andes the radar observes.

Tools
NASA data (NISAR radar and FIRMS heat hotspots).

Why is it creative?
It doesn’t stop at showing a map: it turns the radar signal into a natural recipe for each zone and carries it all the way to the farm through radio and the minka. Rikchay means to awaken in Quechua.

What we took into account

  • No made-up data: when evidence is missing, we ask for field verification.
  • Simple language, in Spanish and Quechua, for rural areas.
  • Only plants native to the Andes.
